name: github-growth

# GitHub Growth

Treat GitHub growth as useful software becoming easier to understand, try, trust, share, and improve. Stars are one discovery signal; they are not proof of adoption, community health, or product value.

## Establish the repository decision

Identify:

- what the project does and who can use it now;
- the intended developer or operator and their use situation;
- installation, access, platform, and license constraints;
- the strongest working example or demonstration;
- current repository assets, releases, usage evidence, and contributor activity;
- the immediate bottleneck: comprehension, setup, trust, discovery, activation, support, or contribution;
- whether the deliverable is a strategy, todo plan, README brief, release package, community response, launch package, or revision.

Use only repository and project facts supplied or inspected. Never invent stars, downloads, contributors, users, benchmarks, endorsements, compatibility, security properties, or maintainer capacity.

## Make the repository ready

Before expanding discovery, ensure a qualified visitor can answer:

- What does this project do and why is it useful?
- Can I see a credible example or result?
- How do I install or try it successfully?
- What are its limits, requirements, and license?
- Where do I get help or report a problem?
- How can I contribute, and what behavior is expected?
- Who maintains it and how active is the project?

Recommend only files and processes appropriate to the project. Common assets include a README, license, contributing guide, code of conduct, security policy, issue or pull-request templates, support path, examples, changelog, and releases. Do not require decorative badges, GIFs, a fixed README length, or a universal section order.

## Build the growth strategy

Choose a small set of connected growth jobs:

- repository conversion: improve comprehension and successful first use;
- release communication: make a meaningful change easy to evaluate;
- developer education: teach a real workflow or technical decision;
- community discovery: contribute usefully where the problem is already discussed;
- ecosystem distribution: integrations, packages, examples, templates, or compatible projects;
- contributor experience: make issues, scope, review, and recognition understandable;
- retention: help users update, troubleshoot, and return.

For each job, define the audience, evidence, deliverable, distribution path, intended action, and review signal. Use the relevant channel Skill for Hacker News, Reddit, Product Hunt, X, SEO, or other off-GitHub publishing instead of copying one launch message everywhere.

Do not claim knowledge of GitHub Trending thresholds, regional star ratios, required launch times, or star velocity formulas. Treat timing and channel sequence as project-specific tests.

## Turn strategy into todos

Make every todo a finishable artifact or test, such as:

- audit the first-use path and document failed steps;
- rewrite a named README section using verified product facts;
- create one reproducible example or quickstart;
- prepare one release note and demo package;
- define contributor-ready issues with scope and acceptance criteria;
- publish one technical explanation through the appropriate channel;
- review repository traffic, successful setup, issues, discussions, and contributions;
- decide what to improve, repeat, or stop.

Include the source facts, intended developer, deliverable, owner-ready output, and completion check. Avoid vague todos such as “get stars,” “post everywhere,” or “engage developers.”

## Write repository and launch deliverables

### README or repository brief

Lead with what the software does, why it is useful, and a credible path to first success. Use accurate commands and examples only when supplied or verified. State maturity and limitations plainly. Move deep material into appropriate documentation when that improves onboarding.

### Release package

Explain what changed, who benefits, why it matters, how to try it, compatibility or migration considerations, and known limitations. Distinguish a meaningful release from a repackaged announcement.

### Community post or reply

Write for the selected community's norms. Share technical value, implementation detail, evidence, and tradeoffs. Disclose the maintainer relationship. Answer the actual question rather than dropping a repository link into unrelated discussions.

### Contributor package

Make the contribution path concrete: setup, issue scope, expected behavior, review process, and help channel. Do not use contributors as a free marketing or support workforce.

## Measure meaningful progress

Choose signals that match the bottleneck. These may include repository visits, documentation paths, successful setup, package use, releases adopted, issues with reproducible detail, discussions, pull requests, repeat contributors, response time, and downstream projects. Use stars alongside these signals, not alone.

Do not invent numeric goals without a baseline. Define what each signal would cause the team to continue, improve, pause, or change.

## Protect platform and community integrity

Do not use fake accounts, automated or purchased stars, incentives for inauthentic engagement, engagement exchanges, bulk promotional issues, scraped competitor followers, or unsolicited mass messages. Promotion inside GitHub must remain related to the hosted project and must not disrupt other users' repositories.

When platform behavior matters, verify current official guidance:

- Repository best practices: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/best-practices-for-repositories
- Repository README guidance: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes
- Community profiles: https://docs.github.com/en/communities/setting-up-your-project-for-healthy-contributions/about-community-profiles-for-public-repositories
- Acceptable Use Policies: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/acceptable-use-policies/github-acceptable-use-policies

## Revise and check

Apply feedback to the named element while preserving verified technical facts and community constraints. If a requested tactic depends on an undocumented algorithm or inauthentic activity, explain the problem and offer a useful-adoption alternative.

Before delivery, confirm that the output:

- addresses the current repository bottleneck;
- is accurate enough for a developer to act on;
- connects discovery to successful use or contribution;
- defines a concrete artifact and review signal;
- avoids ranking myths, artificial stars, spam, and fabricated proof.
